rows.stem:
To balance the following chemical equation, the values of the coefficients \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\) must be respectively :

\(x\,\mathrm{Zn(NO_3)_2} \xrightarrow{\Delta} y\,\mathrm{ZnO} + z\,\mathrm{NO_2} + \mathrm{O_2}\)
rows.solution:
Balance zinc and nitrogen first. Two \(\mathrm{Zn(NO_3)_2}\) give 2 ZnO and carry 4 N atoms, so they give 4 \(\mathrm{NO_2}\):

\(\mathrm{2Zn(NO_3)_2 \xrightarrow{\text{heat}} 2ZnO + 4NO_2 + O_2}\)

Check: Zn 2 = 2; N 4 = 4; O 12 on the left, and \(2 + 8 + 2 = 12\) on the right.

So x, y, z are 2, 2, 4, which is option (C) 2, 2, 4.

rows.stem: Which of the following is a redox reaction, but *not* a combination reaction ?
rows.solution:
In \(\mathrm{Fe_2O_3 + 3CO \rightarrow 2Fe + 3CO_2}\), iron oxide loses oxygen (it is reduced) and carbon monoxide gains oxygen (it is oxidised), so it is a redox reaction. Two reactants give two products, so it is not a combination reaction.

Each of the other three reactions is a redox reaction in which two substances combine to form a single product, so each is also a combination reaction.

This is option (D) \(\mathrm{Fe_2O_3 + 3\,CO \rightarrow 2\,Fe + 3\,CO_2}\).

rows.stem: The salt present in tooth enamel is :
rows.solution:
Tooth enamel, the hardest substance in the body, is made of calcium phosphate. It is not affected by water but is corroded when the pH in the mouth falls below 5.5.

This is option (A) Calcium phosphate.

rows.stem: An aqueous solution of sodium chloride is prepared in distilled water. The pH of this solution is :
rows.solution:
Sodium chloride is the salt of a strong acid (hydrochloric acid) and a strong base (sodium hydroxide), so its solution in distilled water is neutral, with pH 7.

This is option (C) 7.

rows.stem: A metal ‘X’ is used in thermit process. When ‘X’ is heated with oxygen, it gives an oxide ‘Y’, which is amphoteric in nature. ‘X’ and ‘Y’ respectively are :
rows.solution:
Aluminium is used in the thermit process, where it reduces iron oxide:

\(\mathrm{Fe_2O_3 + 2Al \rightarrow Al_2O_3 + 2Fe}\) + heat

Aluminium burns in oxygen to give aluminium oxide, \(\mathrm{4Al + 3O_2 \rightarrow 2Al_2O_3}\), which reacts with both acids and bases, so it is amphoteric.

This is option (B) \(\mathrm{Al, Al_2O_3}\).

rows.stem: The process in which transport of soluble products of photosynthesis takes place in plants is known as :
rows.solution:
The transport of the soluble products of photosynthesis (food) from the leaves to other parts of the plant, through the phloem, is called translocation. (Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from the aerial parts.)

This is option (D) Translocation.

rows.stem: The correct sequence of events when someone’s hand touches a hot object unconsciously :

options.label: A
options.text: Receptors in skin \(\rightarrow\) Motor neuron \(\rightarrow\) Relay neuron \(\rightarrow\) Sensory neuron \(\rightarrow\) Effector muscle in arm

options.label: B
options.text: Receptors in skin \(\rightarrow\) Relay neuron \(\rightarrow\) Sensory neuron \(\rightarrow\) Motor neuron \(\rightarrow\) Effector muscle in arm

options.label: C
options.text: Receptors in skin \(\rightarrow\) Sensory neuron \(\rightarrow\) Relay neuron \(\rightarrow\) Motor neuron \(\rightarrow\) Effector muscle in arm

options.label: D
options.text: Receptors in skin \(\rightarrow\) Sensory neuron \(\rightarrow\) Effector muscle in arm \(\rightarrow\) Motor neuron \(\rightarrow\) Relay neuron

rows.solution:
In a reflex arc the stimulus is picked up by the receptors in the skin, carried by the sensory neuron to the spinal cord, passed on by the relay neuron to the motor neuron, and carried by the motor neuron to the effector muscle in the arm, which pulls the hand away.

This is option (C) Receptors in skin \(\rightarrow\) Sensory neuron \(\rightarrow\) Relay neuron \(\rightarrow\) Motor neuron \(\rightarrow\) Effector muscle in arm.

rows.stem: Sense organ in which olfactory receptors are present is :
rows.solution:
Olfactory receptors detect smell, and they are present in the nose. (Gustatory receptors in the tongue detect taste.)

This is option (A) Nose.

rows.stem: The *incorrect* statement about placenta is :

options.label: A
options.text: It is a disc embedded in the uterine wall.

options.label: B
options.text: It contains villi on the embryo’s side of the tissue.

options.label: C
options.text: It has a very small surface area for glucose and oxygen to pass from mother to the embryo.

options.label: D
options.text: The embryo gets nutrition from the mother’s blood through it.

rows.solution:
The placenta is a disc embedded in the uterine wall. It has villi on the embryo's side, which give it a very large surface area for glucose and oxygen to pass from the mother's blood to the embryo. So the statement about a very small surface area is wrong.

The incorrect statement is option (C) It has a very small surface area for glucose and oxygen to pass from mother to the embryo.

rows.stem:
Select from the following the conditions responsible for the rapid spread of bread mould on a slice of bread :

(i) Formation of large number of spores

(ii) Presence of moisture and nutrients in bread

(iii) Low temperature

(iv) Presence of hyphae
rows.solution:
Bread mould spreads quickly because it forms a large number of spores, which are carried easily and germinate wherever they land, and because moist bread rich in nutrients lets them grow fast. Low temperature slows growth rather than speeding it, and the hyphae are part of the mould's structure, not a condition for its spread.

This is option (A) (i) and (ii).

rows.stem: How will the image formed by a convex lens be affected, if the upper half of the lens is wrapped with a black paper ?

options.label: A
options.text: The size of the image formed will be one-half of the size of the image due to complete lens.

options.label: B
options.text: The image of upper half of the object will not be formed.

options.label: C
options.text: The brightness of the image will reduce.

options.label: D
options.text: The lower half of the inverted image will not be formed.

rows.solution:
Every part of a lens forms a complete image of the object, since rays from each point of the object pass through every part of the lens. Covering the upper half still leaves the lower half to form the full image, but only half as much light now reaches it.

So the image is complete and of the same size, but less bright. This is option (C) The brightness of the image will reduce.

rows.chapter: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
rows.stem: The phenomena of light involved in the formation of rainbow are :

options.label: D
options.text: Refraction, dispersion, scattering and total internal reflection

rows.solution:
Sunlight entering a raindrop is first refracted and dispersed into its colours, then reflected inside the drop, and finally refracted again as it comes out of the drop.

This is option (B) Refraction, dispersion and internal reflection.

rows.chapter: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
rows.stem: The colour of light for which the refractive index of glass is minimum, is :
rows.solution:
Red light bends the least on passing through a glass prism, while violet bends the most. The less a colour bends, the smaller the refractive index of glass for it, so the refractive index is minimum for red.

This is option (A) Red.

rows.subtopic: Magnetic Field due to a Solenoid
rows.stem: The current carrying device which produces a magnetic field similar to that of a bar magnet is :
rows.solution:
The field lines of a current-carrying solenoid are like those of a bar magnet: one end of the solenoid acts as a north pole and the other as a south pole.

This is option (C) A solenoid.

rows.stem: A uniform magnetic field exists in the plane of paper as shown in the diagram. In this field, an electron \((\mathrm{e^-})\) and a positron \((\mathrm{p^+})\) enter as shown. The electron and positron experience forces :

options.label: A
options.text: both pointing into the plane of the paper.

options.label: B
options.text: both pointing out of the plane of the paper.

options.label: C
options.text: pointing into the plane of the paper and out of the plane of the paper respectively.

options.label: D
options.text: pointing out of the plane of the paper and into the plane of the paper respectively.

rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the drawing shows four parallel straight field lines with arrowheads, labelled 'Uniform magnetic field', crossed by two straight lines with arrowheads on which the electron e- and the positron p+ sit; the direction of the field and the direction in which each particle moves are given only by these arrowheads and are withheld here, since together they decide the answer. Page idx 8.
rows.solution:
In the diagram the field points to the right, the electron moves down the page and the positron moves up the page.

The direction of conventional current is the direction of motion of a positive charge, and opposite to the motion of a negative charge. So the moving positron is a current up the page, and the electron, moving down, is also a current up the page.

Both are equivalent to a current up the page in a field to the right. By Fleming's left-hand rule (forefinger along the field, middle finger along the current) the thumb points into the plane of the paper for both.

This is option (A) both pointing into the plane of the paper.

rows.stem: Which one of the following is *not* a natural ecosystem ?
rows.solution:
Ponds, grasslands and forests are natural ecosystems. A cropland is made and maintained by human beings, so it is an artificial (man-made) ecosystem.

This is option (D) Cropland ecosystem.

rows.stem:
**Assertion (A) :** Some vegetable oils are healthy.

**Reason (R) :** Vegetable oils generally have long unsaturated carbon chains.
rows.context: For Questions number 17 to 20, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is **not** the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Vegetable oils that contain unsaturated fatty acids are better for health than animal fats, which contain saturated fatty acids, so the Assertion is true. Vegetable oils generally have long unsaturated carbon chains, so the Reason is true, and it is exactly why such oils are considered healthy.

The Reason is true and explains the Assertion. This is option (A).

rows.stem:
**Assertion (A) :** Sex of the children will be determined by what they inherit from their mother.

**Reason (R) :** Women have XX sex chromosomes.
rows.context: For Questions number 17 to 20, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is **not** the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
The mother has XX sex chromosomes, so every child receives an X from her. The sex of the child depends on whether it inherits an X or a Y chromosome from the father, so the Assertion is false. Women do have XX sex chromosomes, so the Reason is true.

The Assertion is false while the Reason is true, which is option (D).

rows.stem:
**Assertion (A) :** Electrons move from lower potential to higher potential in a conductor.

**Reason (R) :** A dry cell maintains electric potential difference across the ends of a conductor.
rows.context: For Questions number 17 to 20, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is **not** the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Electrons are negatively charged, so in a conductor they flow from the lower potential to the higher potential (opposite to conventional current). The Assertion is true. A dry cell does maintain a potential difference across the ends of a conductor, so the Reason is true.

But the Reason only says how the potential difference is maintained; it does not explain why electrons move towards the higher potential (their negative charge). Both are true and the Reason is not the correct explanation, which is option (B).

rows.stem:
**Assertion (A) :** Ozone layer protects the surface of the Earth from harmful UV radiations.

**Reason (R) :** Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) are responsible for depletion of ozone layer.
rows.context: For Questions number 17 to 20, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is **not** the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
The ozone layer shields the surface of the Earth from the harmful ultraviolet radiation of the sun, so the Assertion is true. CFCs are responsible for the depletion of the ozone layer, so the Reason is also true.

But the Reason tells us what destroys the ozone layer, not why the layer protects the Earth. Both are true and the Reason is not the correct explanation, which is option (B).

rows.stem: Copper powder is taken in a china dish and heated over a burner. Name the product formed and state its colour. Write the chemical equation for the reaction involved.
rows.solution:
Copper combines with oxygen of the air on heating to form copper(II) oxide, which is black. The brown surface of the copper powder turns black.

\(\mathrm{2Cu + O_2 \xrightarrow{\text{heat}} 2CuO}\)

rows.stem: Write chemical equation for the chemical reaction which occurs when the aqueous solutions of barium chloride and sodium sulphate react together. Write the symbols of the ions present in the compound precipitated in the reaction.
rows.solution:
Barium chloride and sodium sulphate exchange ions, and a white precipitate of barium sulphate forms (a double displacement reaction):

\(\mathrm{BaCl_2(aq) + Na_2SO_4(aq) \rightarrow BaSO_4(s) + 2NaCl(aq)}\)

The precipitate, barium sulphate, contains the ions \(\mathrm{Ba^{2+}}\) and \(\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}\).

rows.stem: The melting and boiling points of carbon compounds are generally low and they are largely non-conductors of electricity. State two conclusions based on these two properties.
rows.solution:
1. Low melting and boiling points: the forces of attraction between the molecules of carbon compounds are weak.

2. Poor conductors of electricity: the bonding in these compounds does not give rise to any ions. Covalent bonds are formed by sharing electrons, so no charged particles are formed.

rows.stem: Sometimes while running, the athletes suffer from muscle cramps. Why ? How is the respiration in this case different from aerobic respiration ?
rows.solution:
During hard running the muscles need energy faster than oxygen can be supplied to them. The muscle cells then respire without enough oxygen, and pyruvate is converted to lactic acid. The build-up of lactic acid in the muscles causes cramps.

Difference: aerobic respiration takes place in the presence of oxygen and breaks glucose down completely to carbon dioxide, water and much energy; the respiration here takes place for lack of oxygen and gives lactic acid and less energy.

rows.stem: Write the other name given to lymph. State its two functions.
rows.solution:
Lymph is also called tissue fluid (extracellular fluid).

Functions (any two): it carries digested and absorbed fats from the intestine; it drains excess fluid from the spaces between cells back into the blood; it helps fight infections.

rows.stem: Some unicellular organisms such as Plasmodium and Leishmania differ in the manner in which they reproduce. Name and explain the reproductive process taking place in them.
rows.solution:
Plasmodium reproduces by multiple fission: the single cell divides into many daughter cells at the same time.

Leishmania reproduces by binary fission: the single cell splits into two daughter cells, and the division takes place in a definite orientation (with respect to the whip-like structure at one end of the cell).

rows.stem:
The heat produced at a point due to concentration of sunlight by a convex lens burns a paper.

(a) Explain why it happens.

(b) Name the term (in the context of the lens used) given to the point at which the paper starts burning. What does the bright spot formed on the paper represent ?
rows.solution:
(a) A convex lens converges the parallel rays of sunlight to a point. The sunlight concentrated at this small spot produces enough heat to burn the paper.

(b) The point is the principal focus of the lens. The bright spot on the paper is the real image of the sun.

rows.stem: An electric source can supply a charge of 500 coulomb. If the current drawn by a device is 25 mA, find the time in which the electric source will be discharged completely.
rows.solution:
Charge \(Q = 500\) C and current \(I = 25\) mA \(= 25 \times 10^{-3}\) A. Since \(Q = I \times t\),

\(t = \dfrac{Q}{I} = \dfrac{500}{25 \times 10^{-3}} = 20000\) s.

The source is discharged completely in 20000 s (about 5.6 hours).

rows.stem: Study the experimental set-up shown in the diagram and write chemical equation for the chemical reaction involved. Name and define the type of reaction. List two other metals which can be used in place of iron to show the same type of reaction with copper sulphate solution.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the experimental set-up (an iron nail hung by a thread in a test tube of copper sulphate solution, clamped to a stand) is given as a labelled drawing; the stem names the reactants only indirectly ('in place of iron', 'with copper sulphate solution'). Page idx 14.
rows.solution:
Iron is more reactive than copper, so the iron nail displaces copper from copper sulphate solution. The nail gets a brown coating of copper and the blue solution turns pale green:

\(\mathrm{Fe(s) + CuSO_4(aq) \rightarrow FeSO_4(aq) + Cu(s)}\)

This is a displacement reaction: a reaction in which a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from a solution of its salt.

Two other metals that can be used in place of iron: zinc and aluminium (magnesium also works; the marking scheme accepts any two of zinc, aluminium, calcium and magnesium).

rows.stem: Name the ore of mercury and state the form in which it is found in nature. Write the chemical equations along with the condition required for the reactions involved in the extraction of mercury from its ore.
rows.solution:
The ore of mercury is cinnabar, HgS. It is found in nature as a sulphide ore.

Mercury is low in the reactivity series. Cinnabar is first heated in air (roasting), which converts it to mercury(II) oxide; on further heating the oxide is reduced to mercury:

\(\mathrm{2HgS(s) + 3O_2(g) \xrightarrow{\text{heat}} 2HgO(s) + 2SO_2(g)}\)

\(\mathrm{2HgO(s) \xrightarrow{\text{heat}} 2Hg(l) + O_2(g)}\)

rows.stem: Taking the example of any two animal hormones along with their gland of secretion, explain how these hormones help (i) in growth and development and (ii) regulate metabolism, in the body.
rows.solution:
(i) Growth and development: growth hormone is secreted by the pituitary gland. It regulates growth and development of the body, stimulating growth in all organs. (Its deficiency in childhood causes dwarfism.)

(ii) Regulating metabolism: thyroxine is secreted by the thyroid gland. It regulates carbohydrate, protein and fat metabolism in the body so as to provide the best balance for growth. (Iodine is needed to make it.)

rows.stem:
Mendel crossed pure tall pea plants (TT) with pure short pea plants (tt) and obtained \(\mathrm{F_1}\) progeny. When the plants of \(\mathrm{F_1}\) progeny were self-pollinated, plants of \(\mathrm{F_2}\) progeny were obtained.

(a) What did the plants of \(\mathrm{F_1}\) progeny look like ? Give their gene combination.

(b) Why could the gene for shortness not be expressed in plants of \(\mathrm{F_1}\) progeny ?

(c) Write the ratio of the plants obtained in \(\mathrm{F_2}\) progeny and state the conclusion that can be drawn from this experiment.
rows.solution:
(a) All the \(\mathrm{F_1}\) plants were tall. Their gene combination is Tt.

(b) The gene for shortness (t) is recessive. It cannot be expressed in the presence of the dominant gene for tallness (T), so a Tt plant is tall.

(c) In the \(\mathrm{F_2}\) progeny, tall : short \(= 3 : 1\) (the gene combinations TT : Tt : tt are \(1 : 2 : 1\)).

Conclusion: tallness is the dominant trait and shortness the recessive trait. The short trait was not lost in \(\mathrm{F_1}\) but only hidden, and reappeared in \(\mathrm{F_2}\).

rows.chapter: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
rows.subtopic: Defects of Vision and their Correction
rows.stem:
Study the diagram given below and answer the questions that follow :

(i) Name the defect of vision depicted in this diagram stating the part of the eye responsible for this condition.

(ii) List two causes of this defect.

(iii) Name the type of lens used to correct this defect and state its role in this case.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the diagram shows an eye with rays drawn into it from a point N' on the axis, and a second point N marked on the same axis; which of N and N' is nearer the eye, and where the rays come to a focus, are given only by the drawing and are withheld here, since they decide which defect is depicted. Page idx 16.
rows.solution:
In the diagram, rays from the nearby point N' come to a focus behind the retina, while the near point of this eye, N, lies farther away.

(i) The defect is hypermetropia (far-sightedness): the person can see distant objects clearly but not nearby ones. The part responsible is the eye lens (its ciliary muscles cannot make it converge enough).

(ii) Causes: the focal length of the eye lens is too long, or the eyeball has become too small.

(iii) It is corrected with a convex (converging) lens of suitable power. The lens provides the additional focusing power needed to form the image of a nearby object on the retina.

rows.chapter: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
rows.stem: What is dispersion of white light ? State its cause. Draw a diagram to show dispersion of a beam of white light by a glass prism.
rows.solution:
The splitting of white light into its constituent colours is called dispersion.

Cause: the different colours of white light bend through different angles with respect to the incident ray as they pass through the prism. Red bends the least and violet the most, so the colours separate.

Diagram: draw a triangular glass prism and a ray of white light falling obliquely on one face. Inside the prism and on leaving it, the light spreads into a band of colours, with red deviated the least (at the top) and violet the most (at the bottom). Label the colours in the order V, I, B, G, Y, O, R and mark the direction of the rays with arrows.

rows.subtopic: Magnetic Field due to a Solenoid
rows.stem:
(a) What happens when a bundle of wires of soft iron is placed inside the coil of a solenoid carrying a steady current ? Name the device obtained. Why is it called so ?

(b) Draw the magnetic field lines inside a current carrying solenoid. What does this pattern of magnetic field lines indicate ?
rows.solution:
(a) The soft iron gets strongly magnetised while the current flows. The device obtained is an electromagnet. It is called so because it behaves as a magnet only as long as current passes through the solenoid.

(b) Draw a solenoid connected to a cell (and a key). Inside the solenoid draw the field lines as parallel straight lines along its axis, with arrows all in the same direction; outside, they curve round from one end to the other, like those of a bar magnet. (Drawing only the parallel lines with arrows, for the inside, is enough.)

The parallel straight lines inside the solenoid show that the magnetic field there is uniform: the same at all points.

rows.stem: Differentiate between food chain and food web. In a food chain consisting of deer, grass and tiger, if the population of deer decreases, what will happen to the population of organisms belonging to the first and third trophic levels ?
rows.solution:
| Food chain | Food web |
|---|---|
| A series of organisms feeding on one another at various trophic levels | A network of interconnected food chains, giving many feeding connections among different organisms |

The food chain is grass \(\rightarrow\) deer \(\rightarrow\) tiger. If the deer population decreases:

1. The population of grass (first trophic level) will increase, since fewer deer feed on it.

2. The population of tigers (third trophic level) will decrease, since they get less food.

rows.stem:
A few crystals of ferrous sulphate were taken in a dry boiling tube and heated. Tiny water droplets were observed in the tube after some time.

(i) From where did these water droplets appear ? Explain.

(ii) What colour change will be observed during heating ?

(iii) How many molecules of water are attached per molecule of \(\mathrm{FeSO_4}\) crystal ? Write the molecular formula of crystalline forms of (I) Copper sulphate, and (II) Sodium carbonate.

(iv) State how is Plaster of Paris obtained from gypsum. Write two uses of Plaster of Paris.
rows.solution:
(i) The water droplets come from the crystals themselves. Ferrous sulphate crystals contain water of crystallisation, and on heating this water is driven off and condenses as droplets on the cooler part of the tube:

\(\mathrm{FeSO_4 \cdot 7H_2O \xrightarrow{\text{heat}} FeSO_4 + 7H_2O}\)

(ii) The green crystals turn white as they lose their water. (On stronger heating the solid decomposes and turns brown.)

(iii) Seven: \(\mathrm{FeSO_4 \cdot 7H_2O}\). (I) Copper sulphate: \(\mathrm{CuSO_4 \cdot 5H_2O}\). (II) Sodium carbonate: \(\mathrm{Na_2CO_3 \cdot 10H_2O}\).

(iv) Gypsum is heated at 373 K, when it loses part of its water to give plaster of Paris:

\(\mathrm{CaSO_4 \cdot 2H_2O \xrightarrow{373\,K} CaSO_4 \cdot \frac{1}{2}H_2O + 1\frac{1}{2}H_2O}\)

Uses (any two): for supporting fractured bones in the right position; for making toys and materials for decoration; for making surfaces smooth.

rows.subtopic: Common Salt and Chemicals from It
rows.stem:
An acid ‘X’ present in tamarind when mixed with ‘Y’, produces a mixture ‘Z’. ‘Z’ on addition to a dough when heated makes cakes soft and spongy. ‘Y’ is prepared from common salt and helps in faster cooking.

(i) Write the common names of ‘X’, ‘Y’ and ‘Z’, and the chemical formula of ‘Y’.

(ii) How is ‘Y’ prepared and how does it help in making cakes soft and spongy ? Illustrate the reaction with suitable chemical equation.

(iii) Write the name and chemical formula of a mild base other than ‘Y’ used as an antacid.
rows.solution:
(i) X is tartaric acid, Y is baking soda and Z is baking powder. The chemical formula of baking soda is \(\mathrm{NaHCO_3}\).

(ii) Baking soda is prepared from sodium chloride: carbon dioxide and ammonia are passed through cold brine, and sodium hydrogen carbonate separates out.

\(\mathrm{NaCl + H_2O + CO_2 + NH_3 \rightarrow NH_4Cl + NaHCO_3}\)

In baking powder, baking soda is mixed with tartaric acid. When the powder is heated or mixed with water, the acid reacts with the baking soda and carbon dioxide is released:

\(\mathrm{NaHCO_3 + H^+ \rightarrow CO_2 + H_2O}\) + sodium salt of the acid

The carbon dioxide released during heating makes the dough rise, so the cake becomes soft and spongy. (The tartaric acid also neutralises the sodium carbonate that heating alone would leave, so the cake does not taste bitter.)

(iii) Magnesium hydroxide, \(\mathrm{Mg(OH)_2}\) (milk of magnesia).

rows.stem: Design an experiment to demonstrate that carbon dioxide is essential for photosynthesis. Write the observation and conclusion of the experiment.
rows.solution:
Experiment:

1. Take two healthy potted plants, A and B, of nearly the same size.

2. Keep them in a dark room for three days so that all the starch in their leaves is used up (destarching).

3. Place a watch glass containing potassium hydroxide beside plant A but not beside plant B. (Potassium hydroxide absorbs carbon dioxide.)

4. Cover each plant with a separate bell jar, and seal the bottom of the jars with Vaseline so that no air can enter.

5. Keep both plants in sunlight for about two hours.

6. Pluck a leaf from each plant and test it for starch: boil it in alcohol to remove the chlorophyll, wash it, and add iodine solution.

Observation: the leaf of plant A (with potassium hydroxide) does not turn blue-black, while the leaf of plant B turns blue-black.

Conclusion: in jar A the potassium hydroxide absorbed the carbon dioxide, so no starch was made and photosynthesis did not take place. So carbon dioxide is essential for photosynthesis.

rows.stem:
(i) In the experimental set-up shown above in diagram (I) atmospheric air is being passed into lime water with a syringe while in diagram (II) air is being exhaled into lime water. The time taken for the lime water to turn milky in both the test tubes is different. Give reason.

(ii) Draw the diagram of an open stomatal pore and label (I) Guard cells, and (II) Chloroplast on it. Mention two functions performed by stomata.
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - (i) shows the two set-ups as drawings (I) a syringe pushing air through a tube into lime water and (II) a person blowing through a tube into lime water; the stem states both set-ups in words. Page idx 20.
rows.solution:
(i) The lime water in set-up (I) takes longer to turn milky than that in set-up (II). Lime water turns milky with carbon dioxide, and the air we breathe out contains a much higher percentage of carbon dioxide than atmospheric air.

(ii) Diagram: draw two bean-shaped (kidney-shaped) guard cells facing each other, with the open pore between them, surrounded by epidermal cells. Draw small chloroplasts inside the guard cells. Label (I) the guard cells and (II) a chloroplast.

Functions of stomata: exchange of gases (carbon dioxide and oxygen) for photosynthesis and respiration, and loss of water vapour in transpiration.

rows.stem:
(i) The potential difference across the two ends of a circuit component is decreased to one-third of its initial value, while its resistance remains constant. What change will be observed in the current flowing through it ? Name and state the law which helps us to answer this question.

(ii) Draw a schematic diagram of a circuit consisting of a battery of four \(1{\cdot}5\) V cells, a \(5\,\Omega\) resistor, a \(10\,\Omega\) resistor and a \(15\,\Omega\) resistor and a plug key, all connected in series. Now find (I) the electric current passing through the circuit, and (II) potential difference across the \(10\,\Omega\) resistor when the plug key is closed.
rows.solution:
(i) The current also becomes one-third of its initial value.

Ohm's law: the potential difference across the ends of a conductor is directly proportional to the current flowing through it, provided its temperature remains the same, \(V = IR\). With R constant, \(I = \dfrac{V}{R}\), so cutting V to one-third cuts I to one-third.

(ii) Diagram: draw a battery of four cells joined in series (the long plate of each cell joined to the short plate of the next), the \(5\,\Omega\), \(10\,\Omega\) and \(15\,\Omega\) resistors one after another, and a plug key, all in a single loop.

Total voltage \(V = 4 \times 1{\cdot}5 = 6\) V.

Total resistance \(R = 5 + 10 + 15 = 30\,\Omega\).

(I) Current \(I = \dfrac{V}{R} = \dfrac{6}{30} = 0{\cdot}2\) A.

(II) The same current flows through each resistor in series, so the potential difference across the \(10\,\Omega\) resistor is \(V = IR = 0{\cdot}2 \times 10 = 2\) V.

rows.stem:
(i) When is the potential difference between two points said to be 1 volt ?

(ii) A copper wire has a diameter of \(0{\cdot}2\) mm and resistivity of \(1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-8}\,\Omega\) m. What will be the length of this wire to make its resistance \(14\,\Omega\) ? How much does the resistance change, if the diameter of the wire is doubled ?
rows.solution:
(i) The potential difference between two points is 1 volt when 1 joule of work is done to move a charge of 1 coulomb from one point to the other.

(ii) \(d = 0{\cdot}2\) mm \(= 2 \times 10^{-4}\) m, \(\rho = 1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-8}\,\Omega\) m, \(R = 14\,\Omega\), and \(A = \dfrac{\pi d^2}{4}\).

\(R = \dfrac{\rho l}{A} = \dfrac{4\rho l}{\pi d^2}\), so \(l = \dfrac{\pi d^2 R}{4\rho} = \dfrac{22}{7} \times \dfrac{(2 \times 10^{-4})^2 \times 14}{4 \times 1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-8}} = \dfrac{44 \times 4 \times 10^{-8}}{6{\cdot}4 \times 10^{-8}} = 27{\cdot}5\) m.

If the diameter is doubled, the area becomes four times, \(A' = 4A\). Since \(R \propto \dfrac{1}{A}\),

\(R' = \dfrac{R}{4} = \dfrac{14}{4} = 3{\cdot}5\,\Omega\).

The resistance becomes one-fourth: it decreases by \(14 - 3{\cdot}5 = 10{\cdot}5\,\Omega\).

rows.stem: What are hydrocarbons ?
rows.context: Carbon is a versatile element that forms the basis of all living organisms and many of the things we use. A large variety of compounds is formed because of its tetravalency. Compounds of carbon are formed with oxygen, hydrogen, nitrogen, sulphur, chlorine and many other elements.
rows.solution: Hydrocarbons are compounds made up of carbon and hydrogen only.

rows.stem: List two properties by virtue of which carbon can form a large number of compounds.
rows.context: Carbon is a versatile element that forms the basis of all living organisms and many of the things we use. A large variety of compounds is formed because of its tetravalency. Compounds of carbon are formed with oxygen, hydrogen, nitrogen, sulphur, chlorine and many other elements.
rows.solution: Tetravalency (carbon can form bonds with four other atoms) and catenation (carbon can link with other carbon atoms to form long chains, branched chains and rings).

rows.stem: Write the formula of the functional group present in (1) aldehydes, and (2) ketones. Write chemical equation for the reaction that occurs between ethanoic acid and ethanol in the presence of a catalyst.
rows.context: Carbon is a versatile element that forms the basis of all living organisms and many of the things we use. A large variety of compounds is formed because of its tetravalency. Compounds of carbon are formed with oxygen, hydrogen, nitrogen, sulphur, chlorine and many other elements.
rows.solution:
(1) Aldehydes: \(\mathrm{{-}CHO}\) (a carbon double-bonded to oxygen and also joined to a hydrogen).

(2) Ketones: \(\mathrm{{-}CO{-}}\) (a carbon double-bonded to oxygen and joined to carbon atoms on both sides).

Ethanoic acid reacts with ethanol in the presence of an acid catalyst to give an ester, ethyl ethanoate (esterification):

\(\mathrm{CH_3COOH + C_2H_5OH \xrightarrow{\text{acid}} CH_3COOC_2H_5 + H_2O}\)

rows.stem: What are structural isomers ? Write the structures of two isomers of butane \((\mathrm{C_4H_{10}})\).
rows.context: Carbon is a versatile element that forms the basis of all living organisms and many of the things we use. A large variety of compounds is formed because of its tetravalency. Compounds of carbon are formed with oxygen, hydrogen, nitrogen, sulphur, chlorine and many other elements.
rows.solution:
Structural isomers are compounds with the same molecular formula but different structures.

The two isomers of butane, \(\mathrm{C_4H_{10}}\):

1. n-butane, a straight chain of four carbon atoms: \(\mathrm{CH_3{-}CH_2{-}CH_2{-}CH_3}\). In the full structure, the two end carbons each carry three hydrogens and the two middle carbons two each.

2. Isobutane (2-methylpropane), a chain of three carbon atoms with the fourth carbon attached to the middle one: \(\mathrm{CH_3{-}CH(CH_3){-}CH_3}\). In the full structure, the middle carbon carries one hydrogen and each of the other three carbons carries three.

rows.stem: Write the main difference between self-pollination and cross-pollination.
rows.context: Pollination is an important process in sexual reproduction of plants. It is an essential process that facilitates fertilisation in plants. Pollinating agents can be wind, water, insects and birds. Several changes take place in the flower after the fertilization has taken place.
rows.solution: In self-pollination, pollen grains are transferred from the anther to the stigma of the same flower; in cross-pollination, pollen grains are transferred from the anther of one flower to the stigma of another flower.

rows.stem: Name the part of the flower which attracts insects for pollination. What happens to this part after fertilisation ?
rows.context: Pollination is an important process in sexual reproduction of plants. It is an essential process that facilitates fertilisation in plants. Pollinating agents can be wind, water, insects and birds. Several changes take place in the flower after the fertilization has taken place.
rows.solution: The petals attract insects. After fertilisation they dry up and fall off.

rows.stem: Define fertilisation. What is the fate of ovules and the ovary in a flower after fertilisation ?
rows.context: Pollination is an important process in sexual reproduction of plants. It is an essential process that facilitates fertilisation in plants. Pollinating agents can be wind, water, insects and birds. Several changes take place in the flower after the fertilization has taken place.
rows.solution:
Fertilisation is the fusion of the male and female gametes to form a zygote.

After fertilisation, the ovules develop into seeds and the ovary develops into the fruit.

rows.stem: In a germinating seed, which parts are known as future shoot and future root ? Mention the function of cotyledon.
rows.context: Pollination is an important process in sexual reproduction of plants. It is an essential process that facilitates fertilisation in plants. Pollinating agents can be wind, water, insects and birds. Several changes take place in the flower after the fertilization has taken place.
rows.solution:
The plumule is the future shoot and the radicle is the future root.

The cotyledons store food for the developing embryo (and supply it until the seedling can make its own food).

rows.stem: Define the principal axis of a concave mirror.
rows.context: A highly polished surface such as a mirror reflects most of the light falling on it. In our daily life we use two types of mirrors — plane and spherical. The reflecting surface of a spherical mirrors may be curved inwards or outwards. In concave mirrors, reflection takes place from the inner surface, while in convex mirrors reflection takes place from the outer surface.
rows.solution: The principal axis of a concave mirror is the straight line passing through its pole and its centre of curvature.

rows.stem: A ray of light is incident on a concave mirror, parallel to its principal axis. If this ray after reflection from the mirror passes through the principal axis from a point at a distance of 10 cm from the pole of the mirror, find the radius of curvature of the mirror.
rows.context: A highly polished surface such as a mirror reflects most of the light falling on it. In our daily life we use two types of mirrors — plane and spherical. The reflecting surface of a spherical mirrors may be curved inwards or outwards. In concave mirrors, reflection takes place from the inner surface, while in convex mirrors reflection takes place from the outer surface.
rows.solution: A ray parallel to the principal axis passes, after reflection from a concave mirror, through the principal focus. So the focal length is \(f = 10\) cm, and the radius of curvature is \(R = 2f = 20\) cm.

rows.stem: An object is placed at a distance of 10 cm from the pole of a convex mirror of focal length 15 cm. Find the position of the image.
rows.context: A highly polished surface such as a mirror reflects most of the light falling on it. In our daily life we use two types of mirrors — plane and spherical. The reflecting surface of a spherical mirrors may be curved inwards or outwards. In concave mirrors, reflection takes place from the inner surface, while in convex mirrors reflection takes place from the outer surface.
rows.solution:
For a convex mirror, \(u = -10\) cm and \(f = +15\) cm. By the mirror formula \(\dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{u}\),

\(\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{15} + \dfrac{1}{10} = \dfrac{2 + 3}{30} = \dfrac{1}{6}\), so \(v = +6\) cm.

The image is 6 cm behind the mirror (virtual and erect).

rows.stem: A mirror forms a virtual, erect and diminished image of an object. Identify the type of this mirror. Draw a ray diagram to show the image formation in this case.
rows.context: A highly polished surface such as a mirror reflects most of the light falling on it. In our daily life we use two types of mirrors — plane and spherical. The reflecting surface of a spherical mirrors may be curved inwards or outwards. In concave mirrors, reflection takes place from the inner surface, while in convex mirrors reflection takes place from the outer surface.
rows.solution:
A mirror that always forms a virtual, erect and diminished image is a convex (diverging) mirror.

Ray diagram: draw a convex mirror with its pole P, and the principal focus F and centre of curvature C behind it. Place an object AB in front of the mirror. From A draw a ray parallel to the principal axis; after reflection it goes away as if coming from F (show this backwards extension as a dotted line). From A draw a second ray directed towards C; it reflects back along its own path (extended dotted to C). The dotted lines meet behind the mirror at A'. Draw A'B' to the axis: the image lies between P and F, virtual, erect and diminished.

Mark the direction of every ray with arrows.
